title: Quantum Computing Cuts The Size Of Complex Many-fermion Calculations
excerpt: Quantum computing cuts the size of complex many-fermion calculations, extending first-principles quantum many-body system calculations beyond classical limits.
content:
Weijie Du of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and colleagues have developed a new framework to reduce the computational complexity of modeling many-fermion systems, a challenge for both classical and quantum computers. The work introduces a quantum-classical approach that uses simulated annealing to jointly optimize transformations and active-space selections, effectively shrinking the size of calculations while maintaining accuracy.

A key feature is a quantum-assisted ground-state estimator designed for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, operating with low-depth circuits and relaxed accuracy requirements. The researchers demonstrate the framework’s applicability by modeling the nuclear structure of oxygen isotopes, opening a route to tackle complex problems across multiple scientific disciplines.

Natural Orbital Guided Basis Optimization for Fermion Systems

The framework efficiently reduces the size of many-fermion problems, enabling classical solvers to tackle calculations previously beyond their reach by identifying compact single-particle bases. Unlike existing natural orbital iterative approaches, this method simultaneously refines orbital transformations and selects active space orbitals, allowing both the size and composition of the active space to change during the calculation. This coupled continuous-discrete search is particularly valuable for complex many-body problems where computational demands are high.

A key innovation lies in the quantum-assisted ground-state estimator’s focus on approximate information, sufficient to guide the orbital search rather than requiring a fully accurate solution. This relaxed accuracy requirement allows for simpler sampling strategies with reduced computational cost, and by sampling directly from the Hamiltonian-encoding circuit, rather than more complex Hamiltonian functions, the estimator facilitates the use of shallower circuits.

Starting with a complete single-particle basis, the framework progressively reduces the active space toward a target dimension, ensuring the remaining η-fermion space remains tractable for classical solvers. These natural orbitals are obtained by diagonalizing the one-body reduced density matrix (1-RDM), γαβ(U,A), which describes the particle distribution among the orbitals and informs the selection of active single-particle orbitals. However, obtaining an accurate full-space ground-state vector is computationally challenging for large-scale problems, making the construction of a precise 1-RDM impractical.

To overcome this, the researchers developed an iterative approach to identify a compact, energetically favorable active space through NO-guided orbital transformations and active space selections, driven by simulated annealing. Demonstrations of the framework’s applicability using realistic nuclear interactions for oxygen isotopes show it produces accurate ground-state energies and total angular momenta with fewer single-particle orbitals.

The researchers report that future work will explore applications to various many-electron and many-nucleon systems, as well as hadron structure within light-front Hamiltonian approaches, with further developments using machine learning for efficient Hamiltonian sampling and orbital optimization tailored for NISQ implementations.

Simulated Annealing Drives Active Space Selection

The framework’s efficiency stems from a coupled search strategy, simultaneously refining both the orbital transformations and the selection of active orbitals within a quantum many-body problem. This continuous-discrete search, however, presented a computational hurdle, prompting the development of an algorithm that minimizes intensive calculations. To overcome this challenge, the researchers employed inexpensive matrix operations for updating single-particle orbitals, avoiding complex optimization of basis transformation parameters.

They also used occupation-guided stochastic moves for selecting active orbitals, bypassing exhaustive evaluation of all possible combinations. Simulated annealing drives this process, permitting energetically unfavorable moves to escape local minima and explore a wider range of potential solutions.

This adaptive search scheme is designed to improve efficiency by avoiding the combinatorial explosion of possibilities inherent in many-fermion calculations. For problems exceeding the capabilities of classical computers, a quantum-assisted estimator of ground-state energies and wave functions was developed. This estimator uses a Hamiltonian-encoding circuit to sample many-body configurations, which are then used in a classical diagonalization procedure. This approach allows the framework to tackle problems previously inaccessible to classical methods, while remaining within the constraints of near-term quantum hardware.

Natural orbitals, derived from the one-body reduced density matrix, guide this reduction. The diagonal elements of this matrix, representing the occupations of active single-particle orbitals, characterize particle distribution and inform the selection process. This information is helpful to guide the active space basis selection, although the researchers note that the reference could be updated during the search.

The iteration proceeds by updating the working basis and active space through a series of steps, denoted as T, which combines many-body calculations, reduced density matrix construction, natural orbital transformation and active-space updates. Within each iteration, a “Swap” operation replaces an active orbital with an inactive one, guided by “Remove” and “Add” weights. These moves steer the active space toward the target dimension, improving search efficiency compared to exhaustive enumeration of active-orbital subsets.

Following the orbital swap, the active orbitals are interpolated toward their matched natural orbitals, projecting them onto the orthogonal complement of the inactive space. This ensures that the resulting orbitals remain within the defined active space.

“We first interpolate the active orbitals toward their matched NOs in the ambient matrix space,” the researchers write, detailing the process of refining the orbital basis. This careful manipulation of orbitals, guided by the principles of simulated annealing and natural orbital theory, allows the framework to efficiently navigate the complex landscape of many-fermion problems and identify compact, energetically favorable solutions.

Quantum-Assisted Ground-State Estimation for NISQ Devices

The framework’s quantum-assisted estimator relies on circuits with low computational depth, a critical feature for implementation on current quantum hardware. The adaptive search scheme at the core of this work combines simulated annealing with natural-orbital-guided transformations and active-space selections. This method efficiently explores potential configurations, progressively refining the single-particle basis to identify a compact representation of the many-fermion system.

The framework’s ability to identify these compact bases is key to bringing previously intractable problems within the reach of classical computation, while still maintaining an accurate description of the ground state. By jointly optimizing these transformations and selections, the search avoids being trapped in local minima, a common issue in complex optimization problems.

Calculations of oxygen isotopes with realistic nuclear interactions served as a benchmark for the hybrid framework and a purely classical counterpart operating within classically accessible many-body spaces. This specific application demonstrates the framework’s ability to move beyond theoretical development and tackle concrete physical systems. The researchers emphasize that the framework provides a new path toward extending ab initio calculations to larger, strongly interacting many-fermion systems across multiple disciplines.

The workflow begins with an initial single-particle basis and a second-quantized Hamiltonian, then iteratively reduces the active space dimension toward a target value. Throughout this process, the lowest-energy configuration satisfying a defined criterion is retained. This smooth transition between quantum-assisted guidance and classical refinement is a defining characteristic of the approach. The framework’s design circumvents the limitations of exhaustive configuration sampling and elaborate sampling schemes, features that can introduce errors and exacerbate the effects of hardware noise.

By operating with relaxed accuracy requirements, the estimator minimizes these potential issues, offering a promising route to noise-resilient estimation on NISQ devices. This focus on practicality, combined with the efficient adaptive search scheme, positions the framework as a viable tool for tackling complex ab initio many-fermion problems in diverse fields. The research team proposes that this combination of quantum assistance and classical computation opens a new route toward solving problems previously beyond reach, using the capabilities of NISQ devices.

Hamiltonian Encoding and Low-Depth Quantum Circuits

The framework’s efficiency stems from a quantum-assisted ground-state estimator that uses low-depth circuits, a critical feature for execution on current hardware. This approach allows for simpler sampling strategies and minimizes the demands on near-term quantum processors, addressing a key limitation in scaling ab initio calculations. The estimator encodes fermion operators using Boolean masking and constructs a quantum-walk-based block encoding of the Hamiltonian, streamlining the process for NISQ devices.

This design circumvents the need for deep circuits often associated with more complex Hamiltonian functions, offering a pathway toward noise-resilient estimation. The team’s method samples directly from the Hamiltonian-encoding circuit, further reducing circuit complexity and the potential for errors.

This smooth transition between quantum assistance and classical refinement distinguishes the framework from purely quantum or classical approaches. The adaptive search scheme itself is driven by simulated annealing, a technique borrowed from materials science. This process jointly optimizes natural-orbital-guided transformations and active-space selections, effectively refining the computational space. The temperature within the simulated annealing process controls the magnitude of orbital updates, allowing for broad exploration at higher temperatures and fine-tuning at lower temperatures.

By sampling configurations with measurement probabilities exceeding a moderate threshold, the estimator retains only the most promising candidates for further classical analysis. The operators cα† and cβ, defined by the transformed orbitals, preserve the necessary anticommutation relations for accurate fermionic calculations. This careful construction of the Hamiltonian within the reduced active space is essential for maintaining the integrity of the results.

The estimator’s design also allows for the use of easily preparable trial pivots on quantum computers, further simplifying the implementation. By performing classical configuration interaction calculations on the retained configurations, the framework obtains trial ground-state energies and vectors, ultimately selecting the lowest energy state as the best estimate.

This combination of quantum sampling and classical refinement offers a promising route to tackling complex ab initio many-fermion problems across various disciplines. The framework’s ability to reduce the single-particle basis dimension while retaining an accurate ground-state description represents a step toward extending the reach of quantum computing in nuclear physics and beyond.

Oxygen Isotope Calculations Benchmark Hybrid Approach

Calculations of oxygen-19 and oxygen-21 nuclei demonstrate the framework’s ability to achieve results comparable to full-space calculations with significantly reduced computational demands. The research team employed a three-dimensional harmonic-oscillator single-particle (SP) basis, initially retaining the 0d5/2, 1s1/2, and 0d3/2 orbitals, representing a total of 632 few-body matrix elements detailed in Supplementary Material Table S3. This specific choice of isotopes and basis sets provided a concrete system for benchmarking the hybrid quantum-classical approach against established methods.

The framework’s performance was assessed by comparing ground-state energies obtained with different active-space dimensions, specifically |A| = 9, 10, and 11, using a quantum-assisted estimator simulated in a noiseless environment within Qiskit. Results were cross-checked against full configuration interaction (FCI) calculations performed with smaller SP bases, the 0d_(5/2) shell (|A| = 6), the 0d_(5/2)1s_(1/2) shell (|A| = 8), and the complete sd shell (|A| = 12), which provide exact ground-state energies for comparison.

The simulations reveal that the framework’s results at |A| = 11 closely reproduce the exact ground-state energies achieved with the larger, full-space calculation at |A| = 12, demonstrating a substantial reduction in the required basis size without sacrificing accuracy. A sampling threshold of 10–3 was implemented, retaining only those many-body bases with measurement probabilities exceeding this value for subsequent configuration interaction calculations. This selective approach, combined with the framework’s ability to account for correlations among the SP bases, yielded lower ground-state energies compared to bare-truncation methods.

The researchers also observed small differences in ground-state energies between the hybrid and purely classical approaches, attributing these to distinct stochastic trajectories in basis-space exploration and optimization strategies. This dynamic control over the search process is important for efficiently navigating the complex energy landscape and identifying compact bases that preserve an accurate ground-state description.

The researchers note that less-directed sampling can hinder efficient exploration, motivating further improvements to the bottom-up search strategy. The study’s success in modeling oxygen isotopes establishes a foundation for applying this hybrid quantum-classical framework to a wider range of strongly interacting many-fermion systems across disciplines like quantum chemistry, nuclear physics and hadron physics. The framework’s potential to extend ab initio calculations to larger, more complex systems using noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices represents a step toward overcoming the limitations of classical computing in tackling these challenging problems.
